passage: Every Diwali, when the lamps were lit and the sweets came out, Dada Varun told the story again. "The night Harsha was born, the lane was flooded up to the knees. Your father couldn't find an auto, so I walked ahead with the torch, and he carried the bag, and we waded through all the way to the hospital." Harsha mouthed the words along with him, knowing every pause. Cousins rolled their eyes, but Harsha never did. It felt like a rope tied to something solid. "And then you arrived, right on time, hungry and loud," finished Dada. Harsha sat a little straighter every time.

qa.q: What was the lane like the night Harsha was born?
qa.a: Flooded up to the knees.

qa.q: How does Harsha feel each time Dada Varun tells the story?
qa.a: Proud and a sense of belonging. Harsha knows every pause, mouths the words and sits straighter, as if tied to something solid.

qa.q: How could the family keep the story helpful for Harsha as time goes by?
qa.a: By letting Harsha add a part to the telling or ask questions about it, so the story stays about a family that pulls together, not only about the past.

qa.q: How might the cousins see the story differently from Harsha?
qa.a: They may hear it as an old story they have heard many times, while for Harsha it carries a place in the family, as shown by their eye-rolling.

grounding: A child hears the family story of their birth repeatedly and feels a place and sense of belonging.

passage:
"Dada, tell me the shop story," said Divyansh.
"You have heard it a hundred times," said Chinmay.
"Tell it again. Please?"
"Fine. When I was your age, I walked six kilometres each day to school. Then I saved my first coins and opened a little shop, with one shelf and a scale."
"And the sign?"
"I painted it myself, crooked." Dada laughed.
"Today in class," said Divyansh, "the teacher asked what our family does. I said we open the shop before sunrise, and we fix the crooked sign every year."
Chinmay looked at Divyansh for a long moment. "Yes. That's us."

qa.q: How far did Chinmay walk to school each day?
qa.a: Six kilometres.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when telling the class about the family shop?
qa.a: Pride and belonging. Divyansh spoke of the shop and the crooked sign as "we," as if part of the story.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make at the start of the conversation?
qa.a: Chinmay agreed to tell the shop story again, even after a hundred tellings, and shared the details of the shelf, the scale and the crooked sign.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have felt when Divyansh said "we open the shop before sunrise"?
qa.a: Moved and proud, because Divyansh had taken the story on as part of who the family is; Chinmay looked for a long moment and said "That's us."

grounding: A child repeatedly hears what Dada did and feels part of the family through it.

passage: Every Sunday at Gogo's house in Soweto, Thabo, ten, heard the same story. When Grandpa was young, he had walked forty kilometres to his first job with only one pair of shoes, carrying them in his hands so they wouldn't wear out. Thabo's cousin Gabriel rolled his eyes. "We know, Gogo." But Thabo never minded. He liked hearing how Grandpa put the shoes on only at the factory gate. At school, when a teacher asked the class to write about someone they admired, Thabo wrote about Grandpa's shoes. He read it aloud. His voice shook a little at the end. That evening, he told Gogo about it. She squeezed his hand. "You carry him too, now." Thabo felt taller all week.

qa.q: How far did Grandpa walk to his first job?
qa.a: Forty kilometres.

qa.q: How did Thabo feel after Gogo said 'You carry him too, now'?
qa.a: He felt proud and connected, feeling taller all week.

qa.q: How could a teacher use Thabo's story to help other children?
qa.a: The teacher could invite others to share a family story, helping them feel a sense of belonging too.

qa.q: How does Gabriel see the repeated story?
qa.a: Gabriel seems bored by it, rolling his eyes, while Thabo finds it meaningful.

grounding: Shows a child who repeatedly hears a family story about his grandfather and gains a sense of place and belonging.

passage: For the Class 4 project "My Family Story," Santosh stood at the front of the room holding a photo. "I was born during the big floods," he said. "The water came up to the second floor. My mother was in the hospital, and our neighbours carried food to her in a boat made of plastic drums." The class went quiet. Raghav, in the front row, whispered, "Really?" Santosh nodded. "My father tells it every year on my birthday. He says that's why our building is my family too." The teacher asked how that made him feel. Santosh thought. "Like I belong to a lot of people." When he sat down, Raghav leaned over. "My dad has a story about a train. I'll tell you at lunch."

qa.q: How did the neighbours carry food to Santosh's mother?
qa.a: In a boat made of plastic drums.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel about his birth story?
qa.a: He feels proud and connected, like he belongs to a lot of people.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on this project?
qa.a: The teacher could invite each child to share a family story, as Raghav wants to, so everyone feels a sense of belonging.

qa.q: How did Raghav respond to Santosh's story?
qa.a: He was amazed, whispering 'Really?', and wanted to share his own family story at lunch.

grounding: Shows a child who has heard his birth story many times, which gives him a sense of place and belonging.

passage:
Diwali: At Paati Chandrika's house, Shankar, nine, heard the story again. How Thatha started his cycle repair shop with one borrowed spanner, and fixed a doctor's cycle so well the doctor sent the whole street.
A month later: At school, when a boy teased him about his old cycle, Shankar said, "My Thatha fixed cycles for the whole street. This one is special." He didn't feel small at all.
Pongal: Shankar sat next to Paati and said, "Tell the spanner story again." Then, halfway through, he told it himself, with every detail. Paati laughed and wiped her eyes. "Now it's your story too."

qa.q: What did Thatha start his shop with?
qa.a: One borrowed spanner.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when the boy teased him?
qa.a: He didn't feel small at all; he felt proud and confident because of Thatha's story.

qa.q: What would you advise a family that wants children to feel they belong?
qa.a: Tell family stories often, and let children retell them, like Shankar did at Pongal.

qa.q: How did Paati feel when Shankar told the story himself?
qa.a: She was moved and happy, laughing and wiping her eyes.

grounding: Shows a child hearing a family story repeatedly, which gives him pride, a place and a sense of belonging.

passage: Kashish, you want the story again? All right, sit. The night you were born, the rain would not stop and the whole mohalla lost power. Your Nanaji, this same stubborn man, put a torch between his teeth and cycled through knee-deep water to fetch the nurse from Station Road. Twice he fell. Twice he got up. When he came back, soaked like a rat, you were already crying loud enough for the neighbours to cheer. He laughed so hard the torch fell into the bucket. That's why we say you arrived in a hurry and were loved by someone who would not give up. Your Aditi Nani has told you twenty times, and I'll tell you twenty more, because this story is yours.

qa.q: What did Nanaji hold between his teeth?
qa.a: He held a torch between his teeth.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel each time Nani tells this story?
qa.a: Kashish probably feels warm and proud, hearing again about arriving in a hurry and being loved by someone who would not give up.

qa.q: Which choice in the story shows who Nanaji was?
qa.a: Getting up after falling twice and cycling on through the water to fetch the nurse shows he would not give up.

qa.q: How might Nanaji have felt when he came back soaked and heard the baby crying?
qa.a: He was likely relieved and overjoyed, laughing so hard the torch fell into the bucket.

grounding: Shows a grandmother retelling the story of a child's birth night, giving the child a place and a sense of belonging in the family.
